topic_tag: early measurements of heat from the ocean floor
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Few geologists read the reports when they appeared, and ideas about the ocean floor went on as before for another twenty years. Every heat survey since 1960 has opened by re-measuring the two original sites, and an instrument whose readings there differ from the 1930s values by more than a few percent is sent back for repair. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: Every later survey checks its instruments against the 1930s values, so the measurements serve as the field's standard of comparison: "touchstones." "Watersheds" fails because ideas went on as before for twenty years; "sideshows" fails because every survey since 1960 begins with them; "setbacks" fails because their values are trusted enough to judge instruments by.

watersheds.quote: went on as before for another twenty years
watersheds.why: Measurements after which nothing changed were not turning points.

sideshows.quote: Every heat survey since 1960 has opened
sideshows.why: Work every later survey starts from is central, not peripheral.

setbacks.why: Values used to judge whether instruments work are trusted, not ones that misled the field.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Their readings showed several times more heat escaping than the textbooks allowed for a cold, unchanging seabed. Within ten years those textbooks had been rewritten around a restless ocean floor, though later instruments soon found the 1930s numbers too crude to reuse, and no modern survey refers to them. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: Within ten years the readings had led to rewritten textbooks, so they marked a turning point: "watersheds." "Touchstones" fails because the numbers were too crude to reuse and no survey refers to them; "sideshows" fails because they changed the field's textbooks; "setbacks" fails because they moved the field toward its present view.

touchstones.why: Numbers no one reuses are not standards of comparison.

sideshows.why: Work that changed the textbooks was not peripheral.

setbacks.quote: rewritten around a restless ocean floor
setbacks.why: Readings that moved the field to a new view advanced it rather than holding it back.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Their readings, which later surveys matched almost exactly, appeared in a small regional journal while the field was consumed by an argument over drifting continents. Neither team followed up, and when ocean-floor heat became a central question in the 1960s, the researchers who took it up came across the old papers in a library only after publishing their own results. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: The readings were ignored while the field argued about something else and were found only after the later work was done, so they stood off to the side of the field's story: "sideshows." "Touchstones" fails because the 1960s researchers did not use them; "watersheds" fails because they changed nothing; "setbacks" fails because their values were right and misled no one.

touchstones.quote: only after publishing their own results
touchstones.why: Measurements found after the work was done were not used as a standard.

watersheds.why: Work that went unfollowed was not a turning point.

setbacks.why: Correct values did not lead the field astray.

worlds.passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Heat leaking up along the drill pipes made both readings about ten times too low, and the low numbers seemed to confirm what most geologists already believed, that the ocean floor was cold and inert. For three decades, grant committees cited them when turning down proposals to study the seabed's heat, until a 1962 survey found the leak. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
worlds.explanation: Wrong readings confirmed a mistaken view and were used for thirty years to block research, so they held the field back: "setbacks." "Touchstones" fails because values ten times too low are no standard; "watersheds" fails because they confirmed the existing view rather than changing it; "sideshows" fails because they shaped funding decisions for three decades.

touchstones.why: Badly wrong values cannot serve as a standard of comparison.

watersheds.why: Measurements that confirmed the existing view did not mark a turning point.

sideshows.why: Measurements that decided what research was funded were not peripheral.
